content_voiceover: This is the metabolic map of the red cell, and boards love testing the two branch points. The main trunk is anaerobic glycolysis, the Embden-Meyerhof pathway, which generates ATP and 2,3-DPG and is where pyruvate kinase, PK, sits near the bottom. A side branch off glucose-6-phosphate is the hexose monophosphate shunt, driven by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, G6PD. This shunt generates NADPH, which feeds glutathione metabolism, the cell's main antioxidant defense system. When G6PD activity is low, the cell can't regenerate reduced glutathione fast enough under oxidative stress, hemoglobin denatures and precipitates as Heinz bodies, and you get a hemolytic crisis. Contrast that with the glycolytic pathway defects, like pyruvate kinase deficiency, which have variable clinical significance and, importantly, no characteristic morphologic findings on the smear, unlike G6PD deficiency where you can catch Heinz bodies during a crisis. So the exam distinction is: HMP shunt defect equals oxidative hemolysis with Heinz bodies, glycolytic defect equals chronic hemolysis without a specific morphologic clue.
keypoints: HMP shunt (G6PD) → NADPH → glutathione → antioxidant defense
↓G6PD/GSH + oxidative stress → Heinz bodies → hemolytic crisis
Glycolysis (PK) → ATP, 2,3-DPG; PK deficiency = variable severity, no characteristic smear finding
G6PD and PK are the two classic RBC enzymopathies
keypoint_voiceover: Two enzymes to anchor this slide. G6PD drives the hexose monophosphate shunt, making NADPH to keep glutathione reduced, your antioxidant shield. Deficiency leads to Heinz bodies and hemolytic crisis under oxidative stress. Pyruvate kinase drives glycolysis, making ATP, and its deficiency causes hemolysis of variable severity but with no specific smear finding to point to. That contrast, oxidative versus energy-deficiency hemolysis, is the key takeaway.
